transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-15
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Producer), Lena Rodriguez (Praxis Head of ML), Dr. Samir Patel (VP Eng), Jules Park (Praxis Head Communications)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the owner for this conversation. Quick note, Priya is recording for our labcast; we have about 45-60 minutes. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Lena: Hi Maya, all good here. Excited to share some of our story.
[00:09] Samir: Afternoon, thanks for having us. We're finishing up a sprint so apologies if I'm a bit distracted.
[00:15] Priya: Quick mic check, one two. Good.

Summary intro (auto-gen, may be rough): Maya gives context, we talk about Praxis's move from prototype to production with Redwood, trade-offs, security concerns, and measurable outcomes. Some transcription artefacts re: K V cash and SAML spelled out inconsistently.

[02:03] Maya: Lena, maybe start with a 60-second framing: what product at Praxis this touches and why inference economics mattered.
[02:12] Lena: Sure. So we have a clinical decision support overlay, it's a short-form feature that surfaces context-aware suggestions to clinicians during charting. Initially we ran everything on a few GPUs in-house. The cost was okay for prototypes but once we crossed into thousands of interactions per day latency and cost became a blocker — clinicians can't wait. We needed consistent sub 300 millisecond token latencies and predictable monthly costs so product could forecast.
[02:49] Samir: And our internal ops team was, well, we were stretched. We tried auto-scaling k-8s clusters but the tail latencies were all over the place. Also the NVMe cache warmed slowly which messed with continuity on long conversations.

[04:05] Ethan: That's super common. When you say 'tail', are you referring to p95/p99 spikes? What were you seeing?
[04:12] Samir: P95 was fine-ish, like 250ms for short prompts, but p99 shot up to 1.2 seconds during bursty clinic hours. For embeddings batch jobs at night we saw throttled queues that affected nightly analytics--not good.

[05:00] Maya: Walk us through the decision to pilot Redwood — was it latency, price, security, or all of the above?
[05:08] Lena: Honestly all of the above. Security was big — PHI concerns — so we couldn't do multi-tenant hosted until we vetted our options. The Redwood team was helpful because you offered private deployments and a VPC option, plus the Dedicated offering for predictable throughput.
[05:34] Maya: Right, we do private deployments and dedicated pools. Quick note — we can also do per-route policies so you can pin sensitive endpoints to private model variants.

[06:02] Jules: For the marketing side it's interesting how product reliability directly affects adoption. We saw clinicians drop off if the suggestion popped in late. So that was a core metric for us.

[06:45] Ethan: From the engineering side we worked with Praxis on quantization profiles and model variants — smaller model for low-risk suggestions, bigger for high-compliance contexts. We also enabled KV cache prefix caching and some batching for async workflows.
[07:10] Samir: Small aside — when you first mentioned KV cache we misheard it as 'K V cash' in our notes, which is funny. But that caching strategy actually saved us a ton.

[08:02] Lena: Can you talk about the numbers? Before Redwood our per-token costs vs after?
[08:08] Ethan: After we tuned batching and enabled 4-bit quantization profiles on a set of candidate models, Praxis saw roughly 45% unit cost reduction on average for generation workloads. That varied by route — high context routes saved more because of cache hits.
[08:32] Samir: Latency improved too — p50 dropped from ~220ms to ~160ms and p95 from ~250 to ~290? Wait that doesn't make sense. Sorry, let me rephrase: p95 dropped from ~1.2s to under 400ms in peak hours after dedicated capacity.
[08:56] Maya: That's a key point: predictable capacity reduces the right tail. We also implemented smart routing — non-critical traffic goes to cheaper model variants.

[10:15] Lena: On compliance, the SOC 2 and encryption story mattered. Can you recap what Redwood provided for KMS and audit logs?
[10:23] Maya: Yes, for Private we integrate with customer KMS for key material and we ship structured audit logs to your SIEM over a secure forwarder. We also provide role-based controls and SAML SSO for console access. For proof points, we shared an SOC 2 Type II report and a questionnaire — thanks for reviewing it.
[10:48] Samir: That helped procurement move faster. Legal still asked for SLA language; the Dedicated contract had that baked in which was helpful.

[12:00] Priya: This is great content for the labcast — quick, evocative examples help listeners. Lena, what's one anecdote you can share that listeners will relate to? Maybe a clinician story?
[12:12] Lena: Sure — we had a pilot where a nurse used the suggestion to pick a differential diagnosis phrase; it would have taken her 30 seconds to write, suggestion popped in 150 milliseconds and she accepted. She later said it felt like 'an invisible co-pilot.' That anecdote convinced leadership this was worth scaling.

[14:00] Maya: Nice. On technical details, Ethan, any gotchas during onboarding?
[14:05] Ethan: The biggest was tokenization differences across model variants; early on we had mismatched vocabulary causing minor truncations. We set up a compatibility test harness and validation prompts which caught those before rollout. Also the cross-region fallback logic initially routed to a different model variant with different response styles — that required aligning fallback models.
[14:45] Samir: We also learned to pin versions for clinical routes. Rolling updates are fine for non-critical features but for decision support we pin until regression tests pass.

[16:10] Maya: Sounds like you built good guardrails. Did you run any A/B tests on UX to validate that the latency improvements increased adoption?
[16:17] Lena: Yes, we ran a 2-week A/B where variant A used dedicated paths with caching vs variant B on previous infra. Adoption rate improved by 18% in the dedicated arm; completion rates for suggestions were up too.

[18:00] Priya: For the marketing piece, any concerns around patient privacy in the audio? We'll need a signed consent and maybe to scrub PHI from anecdotes.
[18:08] Jules: Agreed. We'll scrub identifiers; clinicians' names will be anonymized. We'll sign the consent form. We prefer a 90-second clip for social channels.

[19:00] Maya: On benchmarks, Ethan mentioned p50/p95. Are you comfortable if we include sanitized numbers in the case study?
[19:07] Samir: Yes, sanitized is fine. Just remove any exact patient volumes but keep percentage improvements.

[20:30] — mid-call discussion about editorial tone — more human, less vendor speak

[23:00] Lena: One more technical note — for nightly batch embeddings we moved to a separate queue on Dedicated and scheduled compute to avoid interfering with latency-sensitive traffic. That separation cut our nightly job times in half.
[23:22] Ethan: Right, logical separation of workloads is a common pattern we recommend.

[25:40] Maya: Competitors question — procurement asked why Redwood vs Anthropic/OpenAI/Hugging Face. Short answer?
[25:47] Samir: For us it was the combination: private deployment, predictable pricing, and operational tooling. Anthropic had a strong model but lacked our desired private deployment path at the time; Hugging Face had model variety but the orchestration burden was higher.

[28:10] Priya: Quick lightning round for soundbites: Lena, one line on 'why Redwood' from product perspective?
[28:18] Lena: 'Redwood gave us predictable inference economics so we could turn a demo into clinician-facing product.'
[28:26] Priya: Samir, one line technical?
[28:29] Samir: 'Predictable tail latencies and a ded-icated pool meant we could meet clinical SLAs.'
[28:36] Jules: Marketing line?
[28:38] Jules: 'Clinicians noticed the difference—the tech became invisible.'

[30:00] — short break for audio editing notes

[32:00] Maya: Final section — lessons learned and advice for teams scaling inference.
[32:08] Ethan: My advice: instrument early, set clear SLOs, segment workloads, and use model variants for cost/quality tradeoffs.
[32:20] Lena: I'd add: involve clinicians in UX tests early; latency matters more than you'd think.

[34:00] Some light cross-talk about future features: prefetching, more granular per-route RBAC, expanded region coverage.

[36:20] Maya: Last thing, any outstanding legal or procurement asks we should know about?
[36:27] Samir: Only a small SLA tweak and confirmation on data retention periods. Procurement asked for a 7-year audit log retention option but we compromised on 3 years for now.

[40:00] Wrap-up
[40:05] Maya: Thank you all. We'll do the next steps — Maya will circulate the consent and a short form for the sound bites. Ethan will send sanitized metrics. Priya will send a draft of the episode outline and the 90s clip.
[40:22] Jules: Thanks everyone. We'll aim to review by Friday.

[41:00] End recording.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — occasional word swaps, proper nouns sometimes misrecognized (Redwood product names and KV cache). Some timestamps approximated.
